title: The Impact of ChatGPT on English Language Learners’ Writing Skills: An Assessment of AI Feedback on Mobile
venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT delivered through a mobile application can improve English as a second language learners’ writing more effectively than traditional teacher feedback. The study focuses specifically on grammar-related writing errors and also investigates students’ attitudes toward using ChatGPT for English grammar learning. The authors position the work as addressing a gap in direct evidence on AI-generated feedback in school-based ESL writing contexts.

The intervention compared two feedback conditions over an eight-week period. In the experimental group, students wrote a 200-word story based on a picture, typed it into the ChatGPT app, and used a structured prompt asking the system to identify grammatical or structural errors, explain them, and provide examples. Students then reviewed the AI feedback and revised their original handwritten stories. In the control group, students completed the same writing task but received teacher feedback and grammar explanations before revising. Pre- and post-tests used picture-based story-writing tasks, and student attitudes toward ChatGPT were measured with a 12-item Likert-scale questionnaire.

Participants were 132 twelfth-grade ESL students aged 18 to 20 in a senior secondary public school in India. All students were Hindi first-language speakers, had studied English for more than 10 years on average, and were familiar with Android phones and internet use. The same researcher served as instructor for both groups. The study therefore took place in a school-based classroom context, with mobile-supported writing feedback embedded into regular instructional sessions.

The main findings were that the ChatGPT group showed significantly greater reduction in several grammatical error categories than the teacher-feedback control group, including errors involving present tense, past tense, progressive, past participle, plural, and possessive forms. Students also reported generally positive attitudes toward ChatGPT, including ease of use, clarity of feedback, enjoyment, confidence, and satisfaction. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can serve as an effective supplement to traditional ESL instruction for writing error correction, though they note the short intervention period, lack of long-term evidence, and variability in feedback quality as constraints on interpretation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with pre/post comparison and a control group, which supports a green rating. However, it uses convenience/purposive sampling, lacks random assignment, gives limited reporting on baseline equivalence and implementation fidelity, and relies on automated error scoring plus post-only attitude data.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant improvements in writing-error outcomes and positive attitudes, but the practical magnitude is unclear because standardized between-group effect sizes are not reported and outcomes are narrow EFL grammar-error measures during active support. Impact appears promising but insufficiently quantified for a higher tier.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT 3.5 mobile app provided automated feedback on senior secondary EFL students’ handwritten picture-based story drafts after students typed them into the app; the system identified grammatical/structural errors, explained them, and supplied example corrections for revision.
ChatGPT was used as a mobile AI writing assistant for English learners to improve grammar and composition accuracy in 200-word story writing through iterative error explanation and revision.
Students interacted with ChatGPT through a prompted conversational interface to obtain individualized grammar explanations and correction guidance during writing practice.
The intervention was delivered through the ChatGPT mobile application on Android phones during repeated one-hour classroom sessions over eight weeks.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental comparison of twelfth-grade ESL students in India (n=132; experimental n=66, control n=66), the ChatGPT mobile feedback group showed significantly fewer writing errors than the teacher-feedback group across targeted grammar categories in picture-based story writing after an eight-week intervention. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant group effect, F(1,65)=13.745, p<.001, and significant pre/post improvement overall, F(1,65)=123.676, p<.001; the paper reports partial eta squared=.860 for the main effect across error categories, but does not provide a direct between-group standardized effect size for the literacy outcome.
finding.measure: Pre/post picture-based 200-word story writing; counts of grammatical errors (present tense, past tense, progressive, past participle, plural, possessive, comparative, superlative) analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.860 for main effect of error categories; direct between-group effect size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT as an AI writing/language tool was associated with improved ESL writing accuracy relative to traditional teacher feedback in 132 twelfth-grade students over eight weeks. The gains were concentrated in reduction of grammar errors during supported revision of picture-based narratives, although the paper notes comparative and superlative errors were lower in the control group for some analyses and provides no standardized effect size for overall writing proficiency.
finding.measure: Writing error reduction in picture-based narrative compositions revised after AI feedback

finding.finding_summary: Post-intervention questionnaire data from 132 students indicated generally positive attitudes toward ChatGPT for English learning, including motivation, enjoyment, confidence, and satisfaction. For example, 77.27% strongly agreed that interacting with ChatGPT made learning enjoyable, 50.0% strongly agreed and 31.82% agreed they felt motivated to practice grammar regularly, and 68.18% strongly agreed they felt more confident in their English writing; however, these are self-reports without validated scale psychometrics or comparison-group analysis.
finding.measure: 12-item Likert questionnaire on enjoyment, motivation, confidence, satisfaction, usability, and recommendation
